5. looking back on my life, there are many moments of solitude that I cherished. late night cigarettes, when the world is dark and you can hear the night. those moments felt like punctuation, like the mostly-empty page between the end of one chapter and the start of the next

1205947128893169665 [2019-12-14] @visakanv 💜 26 🔁 1
6. one way of surveying my personal history is to see it as a sort of yin-yang cycle between solitude (S) and companionship (C). I was born in a big family (C), but the youngest child by a long shot (S). I loved books (C), but had nobody to share them with (S).
↓
1205947532284588033 [2019-12-14] @visakanv 💜 19

↓

↓

↓

↓
1205950665475772416 [2019-12-14] @visakanv 💜 13

1205951065973088256 [2019-12-14] @visakanv 💜 14

1205951423755603968 [2019-12-14] @visakanv 💜 17

title: Twitter fame is a voluntary descent into madness
summary:
Visakan Veerasamy’s line is the one everyone keeps coming back to: choosing to become a public figure is “a voluntary descent into… madness,” basically a “psychological extreme sport with very high odds of injury.” The thread’s energy is people going, yep, this is *exactly* what it feels like—except Patrick McKenzie (@patio11) pops in as the annoying-but-useful counterexample, saying it wouldn’t even crack his “top 10 challenges,” and asking if it’s really harder than marriage or parenting. Visa basically replies: some of us are unusually well-suited, but most people aren’t ready for what the machine does to your brain.

The debate then levels up when David R. MacIver (@DRMacIver) reframes the whole thing: Twitter doesn’t make you a public figure as a binary; it puts everyone on a *gradient* of publicness that shifts so gradually you don’t notice until you’re already “more public.” His practical punchline is that slow-burn follower growth gives you time to build boundaries—whereas spikes can wreck you. From there, Visa adds the dark mechanic: bad-faith actors can “psychologically DDoS” you into a siege mindset. Qiaochu Yuan (@QiaochuYuan) names the trap that makes it self-sustaining: you find a “bit,” attention rewards doubling down, you grow a shell of fans, which attracts a shell of haters who also reward you for being more you-but-worse.

By 2022–2024 the vibe turns into field notes: Visa says being public means volunteering to be people’s punching bag for their inner conflict, and the bigger you get the more you run into the unhinged “0.1% outliers” (his back-of-the-envelope: ~1 in 1000). “Ignore the haters” sounds simple until you realize building filters changes you, and muting starts to feel like becoming an “out of touch monarch.” The whole thesis gets its perfect meme-ending in 2025 when Sam Altman (@sama) jokes that after a decade of trying to build superintelligence, he wakes up to “look i made you into a twink ghibli style haha.” Why care? Because it’s basically a survival guide for anyone flirting with visibility: the upside is reach, the cost is psychic damage—and the bill scales faster than your follower count.
